Part A · Practice set

Practice set: learning from data

Twenty-five questions on the six chapters of Part A, to attempt without notes

This practice set covers Part A: what a model is, linear regression, logistic regression, grading a model, decision trees and boosting. It mixes calculations, charts and tables drawn from the catch records and the clinic data, and statements to judge. Attempt it without notes and with the chapters closed. A timer is there if you want the pressure of a clock, and about an hour is a fair target.

When you press Score my answers at the end, the page shows your score by area and the questions you missed, with links to the sections to revise. It does not show the correct answers. Revise the sections the score points to, try the missed questions again, and attempt the whole set again after a week.

You will need: a pen, paper and a calculator, and what Part A teaches: A1 What a model is, A2 Linear regression, A3 Logistic regression and softmax, A4 Grading a model fairly, A5 Decision trees and A6 Ensembles and boosting. Some calculations use the logarithms of 0.3 and the probability of 0.7.

How to use this set

  • Close the chapters. Keep a pen, paper and a calculator beside you.
  • Choose a time and press Start timer when you begin. Pause it when you leave. The clock counts down, then goes on counting past zero so that you can see how long you took. The timer is optional.
  • Skip a question and return to it if you like. Your answers are saved in this browser as you type.
  • Press Score my answers at the end. The set is scored only then.
Time allowed

Your answers and the timer are saved in this browser only. No data is sent anywhere.

Models and baselines

Question 1Models and baselines

SharkCam predicts a shark's weight from six measurements. The rule is \(\hat y = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + w_3x_3 + w_4x_4 + w_5x_5 + w_6x_6 + b\). A student looks for good dials by brute force. She picks 10 settings per dial and tests all combinations of settings. Her laptop tests 1,000 combinations per second. How many hours does the full search take? Give one decimal place.

Revise A1 A model is a rule with dials and A1 Learning as a search for good dials.

Logistic regression

Question 8Logistic regression

For the made-up grey bamboo sharks, a logistic regression has the score \(z = 0.31\,(L - 53.0)\), where \(L\) is the length in cm. The model's probability of mature is \(\sigma(z)\). Tag 4127, the juvenile from the Juhu rock pool, is 44.0 cm long. What probability of mature does the model give it? Answer as a per cent, as a whole number.

Revise A3 From a score to a probability.

Question 9Logistic regression

The Pima data are published records of 768 women of Pima heritage, measured in the United States. A logistic regression on the training women has the score \(z = 0.04 \times \text{glucose} + 0.09 \times \text{BMI} - 8.3\), with glucose in mg/dl. The decision boundary is where \(z = 0\). A woman on the boundary has glucose 130. What is her BMI? Give one decimal place.

Training women of the Pima data (a few lie outside the frame). Coral diamonds have diabetes, navy dots do not.

Revise A3 Two inputs and a decision boundary.

Question 13Grading a model

SharkCam's made-up dive log has 2,400 frames, one per second. A frame is labelled 1 when the detector reported a shark (199 frames). Cross-validation with five consecutive blocks of the dive gives 85.3%. The lazy model, which always says no shark, scores 91.7%. Which statement is correct?

Decision trees

Question 19Decision trees

The strip shows 20 made-up training sharks, placed by length. The question 'length at most 41.5 cm?' splits them. Gini impurity is \(G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2\), where \(p_k\) are the shares of the classes in a box. The weighted impurity after a split adds the \(G\) of the two sides, weighted by its share of the sharks. What is the drop, which is \(G\) before the split minus the weighted \(G\) after it? Give two decimal places.

Twenty made-up training sharks from the catch table, placed by length.

Revise A5 Scoring a question: Gini impurity.

A tree grown on 614 training women. A leaf shows how many of the training women who end there are without and with diabetes.

Boosting

Question 22Boosting

Boosting predicts the weight of made-up spadenose sharks. The model starts at the average weight, \(F_0 = 0.219\) kg. Tree 1 is a stump. It answers \(+0.144\) kg for sharks longer than 42.15 cm and \(-0.080\) kg for the others. Tree 2 is a stump fitted to what is left. It answers \(+0.161\) kg for sharks longer than 46.15 cm and \(-0.041\) kg for the others. The learning rate \(\eta = 0.3\) scales a tree's answer before it is added. Tag 3305 is 41.0 cm long and weighs 0.228 kg. What is its leftover \(r = y - F_2\) after two trees? Give three decimal places.

Revise A6 Boosting: a new tree fits what is left over.

Finish and score

Press the button when you are done. Blank answers count as missed. The page then locks your answers, shows your score by area and links to the sections to revise. It does not show the correct answers.

Where the numbers come from

  1. The shark questions use the made-up SharkCam catch table: 600 records generated from published length-weight relationships, not field data (primer/data/sharks/catch.csv). Question 13 uses the made-up dive log of 2,400 frames (dive.json).
  2. The lines in questions 3 and 4 are rounded lines fitted to the 268 spadenose records. The curves in questions 6 and 12, the cross-validation in question 13 and the stumps in question 22 are computed from the table. The scores in questions 14, 15 and 16 are the cross-validated scores of the hammerhead detector of chapter A4. The scores in question 11 come from the softmax classifier of chapter A3.
  3. The clinic questions use the Pima data. It is a published dataset of 768 women of Pima heritage, measured in the United States, and is not data from Mumbai. The Mumbai clinic in question 17 is a story. The models in questions 9, 17, 18, 20, 21, 23, 24 and 25 are fitted to the 614 training women with scikit-learn or XGBoost. Woman A is row 31 of the data: glucose 158, BMI 31.6, age 28.
  4. Some numbers are invented for practice. They are the settings and speed in question 1, the 52% in question 2 and the starting values in question 5. The 8 in 100 in question 17 is invented too. The weights in questions 8 and 9 are rounded from fitted values. The script data/make_tables.py reproduces all the other numbers.
  5. The ideas come from chapters A1 to A6, listed at the top of this page.
